items.title: Camille Vivier esculpe la carne
items.content:
EN IMÁGENES

Camille Vivier esculpe la carne

Quedan pocos días para descubrir la primera gran retrospectiva que la Maison Européenne de la Photographie dedica a Camille Vivier en París. Un viaje hipnótico en el que culturistas, marionetas y exvotos compiten por el título de la más bella escultura viviente.


Por Guénola Pellen. Fotografías de Camille Vivier.

Durante más de veinticinco años, la mirada de Camille Vivier se ha desplazado con rara fluidez entre los encargos de moda y la fotografía de Bellas Artes, dos facetas de una misma obsesión: explorar aquello que, dentro de un cuerpo, ya roza la estatuaria. Desde los inicios de su carrera a finales de los años noventa, ha forjado una obra en la que el glamour nunca deja de coquetear con lo insólito, donde la belleza clásica está siempre acechada por un halo de inquietud.
items.excerpt: Only a few days remain to discover the first major retrospective the Maison Européenne de la Photographie devotes to Camille Vivier in Paris. A mesmerising journey in which bodybuilders, puppets and votive candles vie for the title of most beautiful living sculpture.

items.title: ¡Celebremos!»: La fiesta de todos, una fiesta para todos
items.content:
Dos rostros casi desaparecen tras un torbellino de abanicos multicolores, captados en pleno movimiento con un gesto que debe tanto a la danza como al desfile. La escena podría pasar por un despacho de Magnum, tan decididamente apuesta por una composición perfecta. En realidad, fue tomada en 2019 por una fotógrafa de la que, un año antes, nadie había oído hablar. Esa es precisamente la premisa de “¡Celebremos!”: difuminar las generaciones y conservar solo el instante.

Confeti

YellowKorner cumple veinte años, y los ha dedicado a defender una convicción: la fotografía merece ser compartida, para el placer de todos, y no tiene por qué permanecer encerrada en las ferias de arte contemporáneo. Veinte años abriendo galerías por todas partes, desde Burdeos hasta Shanghái (ochenta en la actualidad), ofreciendo impresiones de arte tanto a compradores particulares como a coleccionistas. Para marcar la ocasión, la casa propuso a los fotógrafos un encargo sencillo: envíennos su celebración, la real, la suya, con su pareja, sus amigos, su familia, la de su ciudad natal, la de sus momentos más felices.

Lo primero que sorprende es que no hay dos imágenes iguales. Algunos eligieron la celebración en su sentido más literal: multitudes, confeti, serpentinas. Otros prefirieron representarla de forma oblicua: un cuerpo solitario, un haz de luz, un aliento contenido. La selección abarca ese abanico, como si la palabra “celebración” solo cobrara sentido en plural. Hay puro documental junto a gestos casi coreografiados, calle y estudio, color saturado y un austero blanco y negro. El hilo conductor, fino pero real, es una urgencia compartida: cada fotógrafo parece haber querido capturar algo que, un segundo después, ya habría desaparecido.

La geografía, por su parte, se lee como un viaje alrededor del mundo en veinte fotogramas. Alexandra Buxbaum nos sitúa en Arizona, Olesia Kim en Tiumén, Eleonora Laufer en Buenos Aires, Yevhen Samuchenko en Odesa. En Brighton, Liban Elmi capturó a tres chicos adentrándose en el mar brazo con brazo, de espaldas a la cámara, atrapados en el mismo movimiento. “La risa cruza las fronteras más fácilmente que las palabras”, escribió el fotógrafo en su solicitud, una frase que por sí sola resume el espíritu de la serie. En Nandgaon, Vivek Goyal se sumergió en nubes de polvo de colores durante el festival Holi, donde hombres y mujeres se rocían unos a otros hasta que el pigmento borra todo rostro. “El color se convierte en el lenguaje atemporal de la conexión humana”, escribió. En Saint-Aubin-sur-Mer, Roxane Mo capturó otro registro de la celebración, más cercano al carnaval que al ritual: en “Flamboyer” (“Resplandecer”), una mujer con un vestido de lentejuelas grita de alegría bajo un aro naranja, rodeada por un desfile de disfraces en el festival ecológico Pete the Monkey. La imagen, emblema de la serie, resume por sí sola lo que busca toda la selección: alegría colectiva, sin filtros, llena de color y expresión.

Memoria

Al bajar un piso hacia el espacio de YellowKorner, se abre una temporada completamente distinta, más íntima: la temporada de la memoria que se vende en el mostrador. “Colorful”, la colección de culto que marcó los mejores momentos de YellowKorner, ha sido reeditada y ampliada para una edición confidencial y exclusiva: veinte imágenes a elegir, cada una entregada en su propio estuche dedicado. Laurent Baheux regresa con sus animales africanos, en blanco y negro, sin una pizca de sentimentalismo. Matthieu Ricard suspende a un monje tibetano en meditación, fuera del tiempo, precisamente lo que celebra la galería La Hune en el piso de arriba. Thibaud Poirier archiva su biblioteca del Trinity College, un templo de papel que casi podría pasar por una nave. También se incluyen: Formento+Formento, Pedro Jarque Krebs, Tull & Bruno Morandi, Nicolas Velter, Jakub Polomski, Bernhard Hartmann, Ruslan Bolgov, Ludwig Favre, Nicolas Bets, LDK, Fabien Novarino, Alexandre Fauve, Damien Dufresne, Robbie McIntosh, Mina Mimbu, Andrea Pavan. Una lista de nombres cuyas impresiones suelen estar agotadas, ahora disponibles de nuevo, listas para colgar en su propia pared.
items.excerpt: For its twentieth anniversary, YellowKorner partnered with Blind to launch an international call for entries built around joy and celebration, drawing nearly 2,500 photographs from around the world. Twenty of them were selected by a jury of professionals and are on view at the La Hune gallery-booksh

items.title: Visa pour l’Image: El mundo que «debemos seguir mirando
items.content:
Gracias. El retrato de Stephan Vanfleteren 2018 de Jean-François Leroy está en todas partes de Perpignan. Hace treinta y ocho años, cofundó lo que se ha convertido en una reunión inmisible para la familia del fotoperiodismo. Murió el 31 de agosto, dos días después de la apertura de la edición de este año de Visa pour l’image, “su bebé”.

Esa misma noche, en el ritual de apertura del festival en el Campo Santo, los 2.500 espectadores que asistieron se levantaron a sus pies. Seguido el aplauso. El presidente francés Emmanuel Macron rindió homenaje en una declaración a “la memoria de un periodista apasionado”, “un incansable defensor del fotoperiodismo”.

“Un tributo que habría dicho que no le importaba, pero que se habría movido cada dos minutos”, sonrió Delphine Lelu, su socio de largo tiempo, visiblemente movido. Ella y el resto del equipo del festival están recogiendo donde se fue. “Mantendremos a Visa viva en consonancia con los valores que defiende Jean-François”.

“Una olla de fusión de cultura visual”

Este año de nuevo, Visa pour l’image demostró ser la encrucijada de la profesión: el lugar donde la gente se reúne sobre una bebida en el Café de la Poste, entre dos exposiciones en la Église des Dominicains, en la calidez de los pasillos en el Couvent des Minimes, o en las proyecciones nocturnas para ver el trabajo de los colegas. Visa es un lugar de comunión entre las personas de la imagen.

En su libro legado, Le Devoir de regarder (El deber de mirar), Jean-François Leroy dijo tanto: “Esta cultura visual derrite significa que, cada año, los fotógrafos, que son solitarios el resto del año, se reúnen, se miran unos a otros, e intercambian, de los más establecidos a los principiantes”.

Así Raymond Depardon, una figura imponente que nunca antes había expuesto en las paredes de Perpignan, apareció junto a una generación más joven: Jerôme Gence, Robin Tutenges, Elise Blanchard y Philémon Barbier. Una mezcla feliz, admiración mutua entre dos épocas, un paso de la antorcha entre generaciones. “Visa pour l’image’s mantra, durante treinta y ocho años, ha permanecido el mismo fotógrafo

En una profesión cuya economía es más precaria que nunca, Visa es un faro en la oscuridad, una fuente vital de apoyo. “Lo que más nos importa es distribuir 21 premios por más de 160.000 euros. Eso es una ayuda seria hacia la producción”, señala Delphine Lelu.

Mantener la verdad

Durante casi cuarenta años, más de 220.000 visitantes han venido a mirar el mundo en la cara (see this year’s full program here), tomando el tiempo para pasar de foto a foto, leyendo cada texto introductorio, cada capción. "Jean-François Leroy se paró para aferrarse a la verdad. Eso era todo lo que le importaba. Se preocupaba por mostrar el mundo como es, sin filtros, mientras que también se aseguraba de que la información podría llegar a un público lo más amplio posible", recuerda Delphine Lelu.

La llegada a Visa significa enfrentarse a la mirada de las jóvenes afganas vendidas en matrimonio para apoyar a sus familias (Elise Blanchard), de los sindicatos virtuales en Japón con personajes de manga (Jérôme Gence), sumergirse en las profundidades de los océanos (Laurent Ballesta) tanto como en los intestinos de Chernobyl (Gerd Ludwig).

Llegar a Visa pour l’image significa ver el mundo en su peor, pero también en su mejor momento. Un mundo que “debemos seguir mirando, incluso cuando lo mira es incómodo”, como lo dijo Jean-François Leroy.

“AI ha hecho sospechar imágenes auténticas”

La visa ha sido a menudo removida por círculos institucionales. Las visitas ministeriales son raras, y los subsidios son más bajos comparados con los dados a los Rencontres d’Arles. “Visa pour l’image, eso es sólo cosas de boom-boom”, dijo un asesor en el Ministerio de Cultura.

Como la fotografía marca su bicentenario, el festival Perpignan nos recuerda cada año que el fotoperiodismo no puede ser tratado como un género menor del medio. Bastante lo contrario: esta ha sido la lucha de Visa desde su primera edición, en 1989. Jean-François Leroy lo puso a su manera: “Como si fotografiar una guerra, una familia o una revolución fuera de alguna manera menos noble que fotografiar un limón en una mesa”.

Visa sirve al bien público. La misión del festival para educar a la gente sobre cómo mirar y cómo entender la información nunca ha sido más esencial que hoy. En la era de la inteligencia artificial, las imágenes generadas y las profundas dificultades, aprender a mirar se ha convertido en una prioridad social. “AI ha hecho que las imágenes auténticas sean sospechosas por contaminación”, advirtió Jean-François Leroy.

La semana del festival dedicada a los escolares es preciosa. Debe extenderse a cada escuela, dado lo vital que son las apuestas. Previamente está predestinado. “Mantengo que el mayor valor de Visa pour l’image hoy es esta educación del ojo que nos esforzamos por defender. Las generaciones más jóvenes necesitan aprender a mirar, porque pronto, como adultos y ciudadanos, será su deber hacerlo,” Jean-François

Una educación a través de imágenes que le importaban tanto, como su apoyo a la nueva generación de fotógrafos. “Tu cámara no te hace fotoperiodista. Tu habilidad para construir una historia con una serie de imágenes que tienen un principio, un centro y un fin, eso es lo que te hace fotoperiodista”, escribió en una carta que ahora lee como una especie de testamento. Para pasarla para que el fotoperiodismo y los valores de su testimonio

38o Festival Internacional de Fotoperiodismo de Perpignan, Visa pour l’image, hasta el 13 de septiembre de 2026.

*« Le Devoir de regarder. Histoires et réflexions sur le photojournalisme » (El deber de mirar: Historias y reflexiones sobre el fotoperiodismo), Jean-François Leroy en conversación con Isabelle Fougère, es publicado por Éditions Mkf y disponible por 20 €.
items.excerpt: The 38th edition of the international photojournalism festival in Perpignan was marked by mourning, following the death of its co-founder, Jean-François Leroy. An essential rendezvous for the profession, Visa pour l’image continues to teach us to look the world in the face.

items.title: William Meyers: Beyond the Bully Pulpit
items.content:
In a Brooklyn subway station, William Meyers captured in 2015 a scene of deceptive ordinariness. Beside an elderly man lying on the platform, victim of an epileptic seizure, a woman kneels over him, watching. Her expression holds both urgency and solicitude. How many such gestures go unseen every day, for lack of a witness?

Film and full frame, negative border included: William Meyers’s method is inflexible. He forbids himself any cropping, entrusting his negatives to Chuck Kelton, a master printer whose New York laboratory is one of the last true sanctuaries of traditional silver printing. The monochrome asserts itself. “Black and white, because it’s a somewhat archaic technology, contributes significance,” he says, “like playing Bach on period musical instruments.”

A successive naval air intelligence officer in the United States Navy Reserve, staffer on a Senate subcommittee on poverty and employment, businessman and photography critic for the Wall Street Journal, William Meyers came to photographic practice in his fifties. This passage through American public life permeates every frame.

The photography critic Vicki Goldberg, whom he readily quotes, wrote: “Vision probably draws as much from the life as from the eye, from the heart as well as the brain, from the complexities of personality more than from ingenuity or mastery of craft.” Only a man who has served, deliberated, and moved through the back rooms of public life could photograph democracy with this particular intimacy, neither naive nor cynical.

From this emerges a radical formal decision: to stand in the ranks rather than face the podium. In the essay accompanying the work, journalist Nicole Gelinas notes that the images that persist in her memory are peopled with “backs of heads and shoulders.” William Meyers explains: “By having someone between the camera and the action, I put the viewer of the picture in the audience, recreating the experience of being there, not just showing what it looks like.”


At the City Council hearing in August 2017, a massive silhouette interposes itself in the foreground, while the room opens behind it onto portraits of George Washington and the Marquis de Lafayette, television cameramen, journalists, and rows of citizens come to testify. It is not power that William Meyers seeks to document here, but the vigilance of those who watch over it.

This perspective produces some of his most striking images. On Broadway, a homeless man sleeps on the pavement in front of the closed window of a Victoria’s Secret lingerie store: the face of a mannequin, behind the lowered blinds, looms over the scene. On Madison Avenue in the snow, an inflatable union rat, symbol of American labor protest, doubles itself in the reflection of a glass facade, its claws seemingly threatening a passerby.

“An important aspect of any art is the significant juxtaposition of key elements,” notes William Meyers. “I work at it.” While he claims the influence of Henri Cartier-Bresson, sharing his full-frame discipline, he puts it in service of a civic grammar rather than a mere poetics of the moment.

Civil Society at Work

Civics is organized around seven thematic chapters, two of which did not exist when the project was first shown at the Nailya Alexander Gallery in New York in 2016: “Social Capital” and “Civic Markers.” “I came to believe that democracy was as much a cultural phenomenon as a political one,” the photographer confides, “the markers, both formal and casual, remind us of what we have to be grateful for.”

In “Social Capital,” five of the thirteen images are shot in a place of worship, a synagogue or a church, during a blood drive or a CPR training session. Homeless men are also sheltered on cots. None of these scenes take place in a government office. When the State falls short, citizens step in.

Further on, in the newsroom of the New York Daily News, photographed in March 2015, journalists work at their screens while historic front pages line the walls: “Ford to City: Drop Dead,” “Men Walk on the Moon,” “Who’s a Bum!” Past and present of the news superimpose themselves within a single frame, a reminder that journalism too is a pillar of civic life, fragile, threatened, irreplaceable.


Two images, taken seventeen years apart, trace the book’s horizon. The first, shot in January 2026 on the steps of the Moynihan Courthouse in Manhattan, shows a woman draped in an American flag: she has just been naturalized as an American citizen and looks, says William Meyers, toward “new tomorrows.” The second, taken in May 2009 in Riverside Park, shows Memorial Day wreaths battered by a nocturnal storm.

“The wind-blown memorial wreaths suggest the fragility of their sacrifice,” the photographer adds, “how tenuous their victories and how needful for the living to be mindful.” The future and memory, side by side, without hierarchy. “I have my own political preferences and prejudices,” concedes William Meyers, “but my aim in Civics was not to argue for any particular viewpoints but to concentrate on processes.”

With the same attention and the same distance, he has photographed members of the Westboro Baptist Church, an American sect notoriously known for its hate-filled demonstrations, and a rally in favor of the Ground Zero mosque; the anti-capitalist Occupy Wall Street movement in Zuccotti Park and a march by the deeply conservative Tea Party; a Black Lives Matter banner on Broadway and an assembly standing at an official NYPD promotion ceremony.

Of the Westboro church members, whom he says he detests without reservation, he retains one precise image: “The critical component of the picture is the cop in the foreground who is protecting their right to be despicable. That, and the pedestrians who are exercising their right to ignore them.” Democracy, in this light, is not agreement on values. It is the procedure that allows incompatible convictions to coexist without destroying each other.

Civics by William Meyers is published by Apollo Publishers and available for $50.
items.excerpt: With Civics, the New York photographer draws a portrait of ordinary democracy. An inhabited, grave, and luminous work, arriving as the United States marks its 250th anniversary.

items.title: Photography Takes the Pulse of France
items.content:
A white and pink caravan, parked beneath the colonnades of the Palais-Royal. A little further on, beneath the Arc de Triomphe, the same silhouette, towed by a silent gray SUV. Between the two, a mobile analog photography studio, a traveling darkroom, and this line painted on the side: “Step into the darkroom and reveal the portrait of your heart.” It could pass for a contemporary art installation that wandered off course. It is in fact a touring device, designed to crisscross France for over a year. And yes, visitors leave with an image of their own heart.

The LUX Tour officially launched on September 3, 2026, in the courtyard of the Ministry of Culture, at the Jardin du Palais-Royal in Paris. Behind the name stands the LUX Network, which brings together 33 photography festivals and fairs across the country, from Rennes to Bordeaux, from Nîmes to Boulogne-Billancourt. At the heart of the project (the phrase, here, is more than a figure of speech) sits “À l’origine du cœur,” an artistic experience devised by the Trigone collective.

The principle is almost childlike in its simplicity: visitors have electrodes placed on them, their pulse is captured, converted into an electrical impulse, and that impulse exposes a sheet of light-sensitive paper. The deep red of the darkroom. A graduated cylinder, amber developer poured under the glow of a safelight. Then, on the paper, a white branching form spreads like a bolt of lightning, resembling an upside-down tree, or the vessels of a heart traced by electricity itself. Each print is unique, naturally, like every heartbeat.

BMW France, official partner of the venture, does more than put its logo on the trailer. The brand has provided the Trigone collective with the new BMW iX3, fully electric, tasked with towing the caravan and, thanks to its bidirectional Vehicle-to-Load charging technology, powering some of the mobile studio’s equipment. Electricity, in effect, runs through every layer of the project.

There is, in this story, a coincidence BMW is happy to point out. Nicéphore Niépce, the inventor of photography, was also, together with his brother Claude, behind one of the earliest internal combustion engines. Two centuries later, image and mobility find themselves on the same trailer. “This unexpected link between image and mobility resonates strongly with our commitment to the LUX Network,” says Vincent Salimon, chairman of the board of BMW Group France, adding: “We are proud to support a project that brings together heritage, innovation, contemporary creation and the regions.”

The project itself did not begin yesterday. It started at ETPA, the Toulouse photography school, where Paul Baudon built a device capable of amplifying the heart’s electrical signal to trigger an arc that spreads across analog paper. The Trigone collective, which he formed with Anthony Jean and Marianne Thazet, took up the idea in 2021 and has since toured towns, villages and festivals aboard an earlier mobile lab, well before the BMW chapter. Their acknowledged references bring together two figures: the astronomer and illustrator Étienne-Léopold Trouvelot, a pioneer in depicting electrical phenomena in the 19th century, and Hiroshi Sugimoto, whose Lightning Fields series likewise captures electricity directly on film. “A heartbeat is caused by an electrical impulse,” sums up Paul Baudon, adding that the aim is to “materialize the invisible,” the rhythm of life in its most organic form.

From Rennes to Deauville, from Clermont-Ferrand to Céret, the caravan is set to stop at major dates on the French photography calendar, Paris Photo, La Gacilly, the off-circuit of the Rencontres d’Arles, the Mulhouse Biennale, before returning to Paris for Photoclimat in September 2027, exactly a year after its launch. The LUX Tour is in fact just one of three strands of the 200LUX program, labeled part of the Bicentennial of Photography by the Ministry of Culture: alongside it, a Dictionnaire (presque) complet de la photographie (Almost Complete Dictionary of Photography), an editorial project tracing two centuries of history through the eyes of the network’s members, and a group exhibition of all 33 festivals at the MAC, Maison des Arts de Créteil.

Looking at the Trigone collective’s images, one thinks of old X-rays, of laboratory lightning, of the electrical branchings once known as Lichtenberg figures. Inside the caravan, the experience is intense. Once the session ends, the print follows the classic analog path: development, scanning and printing, before being handed to the visitor as a trace of their passage. Everything relies on chemistry and on the operator’s hand, which, for a device designed to run for 13 months across 33 stops, amounts to as much a logistical feat as an artistic one.

More information on the LUX Tour, including full dates and stops, is available here.
items.excerpt: BMW France partners with the LUX Network to bring “À l’origine du cœur” (At the Heart’s Origin), the photographic experience by the Trigone collective, to 33 French festivals. A caravan, an analog studio, a heartbeat turned into an image: the Bicentennial of Photography hits the road until September

items.title: Reap the Earth, Feed Kyoto
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Reap the Earth, Feed Kyoto

Kyoto Farm to Table traces the living roots of Japan’s former capital, where the farmer’s gesture meets the plate with an almost sacred rigor.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Viola Gaskell.

This book springs from the meeting of two complementary voices. Viola Gaskell, an American journalist and photographer from Hawaii, and Momoko Nakamura, a Japanese food writer, joined forces to interview more than thirty producers, chefs, fishermen, and tofu makers across Kyoto.

The city sits atop a singular vegetable heritage, the kyō-yasai, grown for over a thousand years in rich soil fed by exceptionally pure water. The round, plump kamonasu eggplant, the slender kujō-negi leek, and the mild shōgoin-daikon radish rank among the varieties most coveted by high-end kitchens.

This land nurtures shizen shoku, farming free of synthetic inputs, where soil regenerates through compost and crop rotation rather than chemical fertilizer. That philosophy feeds in turn into washoku, the Japanese culinary tradition inscribed by UNESCO on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2013.

Each figure met in this book found their own path toward that philosophy. For some, time abroad was the spark; for others, the Fukushima disaster struck like a warning bell, a call to reconsider the bond between land and body.

Gaskell’s eye had already been sharpened elsewhere, on organic farming in China and on Hong Kong’s vanishing cha chaan tengs, Cantonese diners where Western influence meets local flavor. Kyoto offers her a new terrain of rare intimacy.

 

Kyoto Farm to Table, by Viola Gaskell and Momoko Nakamura, is published by Trope and is available for pre-order at $50.

items.title: Vladimir Seleznev : Quiet, We Pray
items.content:
Start with a sentence, a sign Vladimir Seleznev saw a hundred times before he understood it. In a Russian church, worshippers aren’t gently asked to stay quiet during the service. They’re warned. “Those who talk in the temple are consigned to sorrow and woe,” the sign reads. “If you walk into a church in France and someone asks you not to talk during the service, I think in France it would say please don’t talk. In Russia, it’s written like this,” the artist recalls. The phrase is an instruction manual, and the photographer decided to follow it to the letter, turning it into the title of a project carried out between 2018 and 2024.

This isn’t Seleznev’s first attempt at the subject. Ten years ago, his first book already told the story of an imagined city, a future built on the model of Soviet utopias and then abandoned, a ghost city conceived in echo of Le Corbusier wanting to raze the center of Paris. The book was published by Meduza, an opposition outlet now banned in Russia. At the time, a handful of strangers bought it from France. “It was my first book, and in my opinion, it was excellent,” he says, not bothering with false modesty. It’s out of that decade-long project that the next, harsher idea was born: understanding the instruments by which power shapes a people. “What interests me are the instruments the government, the politicians, use to influence people,” he explains. Religion, historical memory, collective representations: the list is short, but it’s enough.

The starting point is an observation owed to Alexei Tolstoy. The writer, in a novel devoted to Ivan the Terrible, noted that what was most striking wasn’t that such a tyrant had existed, but that there could have existed “a society that watched him without indignation.” Seleznev grew up in that very society, in a devout family. “I’m completely materialist myself, but it’s very hard to rid yourself of that system,” he says. The system in question has its statistics: three churches opened every day in Russia, the word God written into the Constitution since 2020, a Criminal Code article that has punished offending believers’ feelings since 2013. It also has its promised martyrs. The Patriarch calls the coronavirus epidemic divine mercy, the president assures that in the event of nuclear war, Russians will go to paradise as martyrs, and in June 2023 the Orthodox Church declared that pacifism is incompatible with its teaching. There is no authority except from God, says the Epistle to the Romans. In Russia, the line has had quite a career.

How do you photograph an ideology that won’t be photographed? Seleznev documents almost nothing. He composes. A wax hand sold as a relic, bought exactly as found. An in-utero baptism, a medieval rite he saw resurface on Russian social media and staged just as described, “because it still exists, it really exists.” A naked man kneeling in the icy January water, a ritual gesture he describes without apology: “Religious people in Russia have this strict idea of always plunging into cold water, maybe you can get sick, it doesn’t matter, they do it anyway.” And those objects of molten wax, halfway between icon and wound, which he shapes himself in his studio by melting and then burning cones, before lighting them with a single flash carried from scene to scene. “Gregory Crewdson has many light sources, I only have one, but I get a great result,” he says.

These distorted icons, torsos split open, faces erased, bear a family resemblance to Lucio Fontana’s slashed canvases, whose religious ceramics the artist discovered only afterward, as a spectator of his own work. “I hadn’t seen that when I was making my photos, but now I can see the connection,” he admits. One also thinks, watching a nighttime procession by a lake where the faithful advance on their knees, candles in hand, of Werner Herzog’s documentary Bells from the Deep, and of the legend of Kitezh, the holy city popular belief says lies sunken, which the faithful expect to see rise again every year. Seleznev doesn’t cite Herzog out of authorial flourish: he re-enacts the gesture, the kneeling, the walk around the lake, before recognizing the connection himself.

He carries the paradox without grandstanding. To dismantle a language, you have to speak it. “I use the visual language of religious painting against religion,” he sums up, before citing a Russian proverb about fighting an enemy with his own weapon. The proverb comes at a cost. Seleznev left Russia in 2022, “not because of the project, because of the war,” he says, though the two soon became inseparable. The Russian curators once interested in his work backed away one by one. “Today it’s even forbidden to exhibit a photo with a church in it if there’s anything not quite ideal standing next to it,” he says. The project has been shown only once, in Portugal, at a photography festival. In France, it produces an effect he hadn’t anticipated: “These photos raise the most questions, I was very surprised,” he says, almost amused that it took crossing Europe for his work to finally start speaking.

His mother, he says, remains a fanatical supporter of Vladimir Putin and the war. His daughter, from a first marriage, much less so. Between the two lies an entire country where, he believes, the image of the president and the image of God have ended up merging, for lack of icons to tell them apart. Seleznev, for his part, chose his side long ago: that of the materialist who cannot stop photographing the very thing he cannot shake off.

items.title: John Baldessari: Language and Image
items.content:
IN IMAGES

John Baldessari: Language and Image

Pérez Art Museum Miami presents “John Baldessari: The End of the Line”, an exhibition tracing the conceptual artist’s rethinking of photography, video, painting, and the relationship between images, words, and meaning.

By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by John Baldessari.

Language was at the center of John Baldessari’s practice, whether expressed through words, photographs, or film stills. In 1970, he burned most of the paintings he had made between 1953 and 1966, turning the act of destruction into the Cremation Project. The gesture shifted attention away from authorship and the artwork as object, toward the act and thought process of making art. Photography and video documented the moment, while in the following decades Baldessari increasingly worked with found photographs, film stills, and images drawn from an ever-expanding archive of popular culture.

Baldessari obscured faces and other details with colored circles, disrupting the original narratives of mass-media images and creating gaps in meaning. His deceptively economical visual language invited viewers to construct their own connections. “I go back and forth between wanting to be abundantly simple and maddeningly complex,” he once said. The tension captures much of what makes his work so compelling: images that appear immediate, yet become increasingly complex the longer the viewer looks and reflects on them.

The exhibition “John Baldessari: The End of the Line” is on view at the Pérez Art Museum Miami until May 9, 2027.

items.title: Madonna Before Madonna
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Madonna Before Madonna

This is a Madonna in her early twenties, still unknown to the public, that Musichead Gallery, on Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, invites us to discover: seven photographers captured her between 1980 and 1985, back when she was still nobody — and already punk to the core.


By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Marc Canter, Richard Corman, Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Mick Rock, and Mark Weiss.

A girl from Michigan lands alone in New York, ready to do whatever it takes to make it on her own terms: drummer, dancer, author of her own songs. Refusing to let the industry claim her, she turns down a ready-made pop career offered in Paris — where others would have written her songs for her — and heads back to New York to co-write them herself. This is the face of that Madonna, punk, sensual, already at war with the establishment, that “The Rise of the Material Girl” reveals.

In the photographs, her style already reads like a manifesto: a red beret tilted just so, a studded belt, leather cuffs and bracelets stacked to the wrist, torn jeans, a look that’s half dare, half play, a lollipop between her lips like a quiet provocation. Worn denim and crimson lipstick, jewelry piled on in layers: the visual vocabulary of an icon, feminine and defiant in the same breath.

Behind the lens: Richard Corman, who met her by chance in 1983 and photographed her in her Lower East Side apartment; Deborah Feingold, who shot the now-iconic “lollipop series” in 1982, in all of twenty minutes; Gary Heery, the Australian photographer working out of Soho, behind some of her earliest publicity photos; and Mark Weiss, who caught her on the set of MTV in 1984. That same year, the album Like a Virgin would catapult Madonna from anonymity to worldwide fame: the legend of the Madonna with Marilyn’s afterglow was underway.

 

“Madonna: The Rise of the Material Girl (1980–1985)” is on view at Musichead Gallery in Los Angeles, through September 26, 2026.

items.title: Meeting the Revolution, One Face at a Time
items.content:
For Amin Yousefi, the project began with a photograph that shouldn’t have mattered. Working through an archive in Tehran during the pandemic, he paused over an image of a student gathering from the years of the Iranian Revolution – not a defining historical moment, but an ordinary crowd. Among its faces, one person looked directly into the camera, carrying the unsettling sensation of being addressed by someone he could never have met. One photograph wasn’t enough to trust that feeling. It was only after encountering it again and again across the revolution’s vast photographic archive that the project began to take shape.

Born in Abadan in 1996, Yousefi was thirteen during the disputed 2009 presidential election and the protests that became known as the Green Movement – old enough to witness one rupture in Iran’s history, but to inherit the revolution itself only through photographs, documentaries and annual commemorations. Rather than retelling its history, he followed that intuition, rephotographing archival images through a magnifying loupe until the encounters themselves became the work. “For me,” he says, “it was more about this encounter.”

Photographs made to record a revolution begin, almost against their own nature, to behave like portraits. What emerges is the quiet reciprocity of photography: anonymous crowds give way to individuals who actively acknowledge the photographer’s presence. For a moment, the revolution recedes behind something quieter: the brief acknowledgement between photographer and subject, before history carries them both away. One enlarged face eventually led Yousefi to its owner: pioneering Iranian photojournalist Hengameh Golestan, captured looking towards American photographer David Burnett as he photographed the revolution. Golestan barely remembered the moment, recalling only that Burnett had been, in her words, “a handsome man.” The anecdote gently unsettles any certainty about who is looking at whom, reminding us that photographs rarely belong to a single perspective.

That ambiguity runs throughout the book. Yousefi resists romanticising the crowds’ desire to be photographed, instead contrasting it with the radically different relationship to visibility today, when surveillance has transformed public space. Here, the people gathered wanted to be seen; contemporary protesters, he observes, often seek the opposite. The book’s design quietly reinforces that tension. Each enlarged photograph faces a page of solid black, isolating the gaze before the sequence gradually pulls back to reveal more of the surrounding scene, until individual faces dissolve once again into the crowd. The experience feels less like turning the pages of a photobook than adjusting one’s own eyesight – moving between intimacy and distance, lucidity and doubt.

Even the title resists certainty. Yousefi has little interest in describing what the book contains, preferring instead a phrase that preserves the ambiguity he found in the archive. “There are so many faces that are not sure,” he says. By the final pages, those eyes have quietly dissolved back into the crowd. What lingers is a fleeting exchange – one person behind a camera, another before it – and the quiet feeling of having briefly met someone who, in that moment, wanted to be seen.

Eyes Dazzle as They Search for the Truth is published by Luhz Press, distributed internationally by Idea Books, and available for €48,95.

items.title: Nick Haymes’s Family, Every Which Way
items.content:
Nick Haymes lived only a couple of blocks from the World Trade Center. Chronograph, published by SPBH Editions / MACK, opens on images of the catastrophe, September 11, 2001, before the subject shifts toward the family unit — intimate terrain Nick Haymes would go on exploring for twenty-five years. From there, Lina, his partner, and later their sons Philipp and Lawrence, overrun every photograph, caught in their trivial, everyday lives as much as in more solemn moments.

The father makes no attempt at the perfect shot. In his pictures, the children often have their eyes shut. A child howls with rage, his mouth full of yoghurt, rather than smiling for the camera. Drool regularly smears the chin, snot runs: in real life, children could not care less about their manners. These images, which a technical eye would call failures, never end up in the bin. Chronograph draws its strength from exactly that: the accident stands in for the truth.

The title borrows from the vocabulary of horology: a chronograph measures the passing of time, minute by minute. Chronograph works in the same register, collecting recurrences — a handful of motifs that return page after page like familiar landmarks. The same nose bleeding under a blue-tiled shower, the same bathtime ritual. One can almost imagine cohabiting within the 800 square feet of their New York apartment, in this endearing, familiar chaos.

The catalogue of small domestic accidents lengthens with every page. A grazed knee, a lost tooth brandished like a trophy, a cut finger, a splint one day, a cast scrawled with doodles the next. A nose bleeds, again, under the shower. One could almost mistake it for war… seen at a child’s height. A sole of a foot, a few warts breaking its surface, even gets its own close-up.

Lina, the children’s mother, regularly appears in frame, sometimes nude or in her underwear, sprawled across an unmade bed or a sofa, never in a studied pose. The children undress just as naturally, unbothered by the lens, alone or curled against her. This shared nakedness escapes the usual modesty of family albums: it speaks of an innocence that precedes self-consciousness, a tender and natural relationship to the body.

Between the two brothers, the camera mostly captures the disorder inherent to siblinghood: silly string flying in white filaments through a ransacked bedroom, a Jenga tower teetering, a quarrel whose shouts one can only guess at. Their father photographs them from every angle, with the same attention paid to each. This disorder also makes room for stillness: a hand resting on a shoulder, a glance seeking another in the middle of a game, never staged and all the truer for it.


Elsewhere, the book gives itself over entirely to farce. A boy bolts naked down a hotel corridor. Another is immortalized urinating in the bathroom, wearing a Mexican wrestling mask. The younger boy, also masked, devours a chocolate cupcake with both hands, his face smeared with chocolate. Blond and curly-haired, he multiplies his antics: grimaces, absurd poses, in a comic generosity all his own.

Rituals return with the same regularity as the scrapes and bruises. One of them stands apart in its gravity: death makes its first, quiet entrance into the book. The family hamster, who appears repeatedly and was often good for a laugh, seemed a full-fledged member of the household. He is buried in a small cardboard coffin, carefully made. A ceremony photographed like reportage, foreshadowing the human losses to come.

The years pass: the children grow up, the adults grow old. Childhood nakedness gives way to a new modesty. On a black-and-white beach, two young men, childhood now firmly behind them, walk bare-chested.


Toward the end of the book, illness settles in without warning on Mikhail Kutsovsky and Nadezhda Kutsovskaya, Philipp and Lawrence’s grandparents, already familiar to the reader from earlier kitchen scenes and family gatherings. They appear undergoing dialysis, hooked to IVs in beige recliners, under the wan glow of fluorescent lights. Further on, one of the boys leans over his bedridden grandmother, his hand resting tenderly on hers.

We find them again in a hospital room, before their final separation. They die a year apart, but the book reunites them one last time, at the burial. In a striking image, two urns rest side by side on a table draped in blue. Philipp and Lawrence each play an important, symbolic role in the ceremony, visibly moved. On a nearby easel stands the photograph of the grandfather holding his grandsons as children, already seen earlier in the book.

A cycle closes here. One leaves this small world reluctantly, closing the book. This family is already missed.

Chronograph by Nick Haymes is published by SPBH Editions / MACK, and is available at £55.

items.title: Inez & Vinoodh: Glamour, Desire, and Subversion
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Inez & Vinoodh: Glamour, Desire, and Subversion

The unsettling body of work by the celebrated Dutch photography duo can be seen until September 6 at Kunstmuseum Den Haag in The Hague (Netherlands), as part of the retrospective “Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh”, or in the book of the same name published by Hannibal Books.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Inez & Vinoodh.

Inez van Lamsweerde (b. 1963) and Vinoodh Matadin (b. 1961), a couple in life as in work since meeting in Amsterdam in 1986, rank among the most influential photography duos of their generation. In December 2023, they created the now-iconic portrait of Taylor Swift, named Person of the Year by Time magazine. The superstar was photographed in New York with her cat, Benjamin Button, draped over her shoulders — a pose inspired by Cat People, a 1978 book by American photographer Bill Hayward, of which Inez had given the singer a vintage copy.

From the 1990s onward, Inez & Vinoodh made their name with digitally retouched fashion photographs, a practice still rare at the time, which they explored well before the Photoshop era. Their sleek, polished aesthetic stood in sharp contrast to the documentary-style grunge look then dominant, embodied by photographers such as Juergen Teller, and found a home in publications like The Face, a cult British fashion and music magazine, and Vogue. While their work goes far beyond simple celebrity commissions, an entire room of the exhibition is devoted to their portraits of pop-culture figures, including actress Tilda Swinton, singer Billie Eilish, model Kate Moss, and singer Rosalía.

Acting as both mirror and magnifying glass, Inez & Vinoodh’s photography draws on popular culture even as it questions it. Beneath the glamour, the grotesque often surfaces, classic gender roles are upended, and an unsettling unheimlich quality — familiar yet disquieting — runs through much of their work. The “Fashion Plate” series, created during lockdown, pairs high jewelry with cut-out fashion images, for Vogue Paris.

The duo also explores nature through botanical still lifes, a practice they have pursued for several years. This strand draws on the Dutch tradition of floral still-life painting, while steering it toward a stranger kind of beauty, somewhere between elegance and oddity. It extends, beyond portraiture, their fascination with metamorphosis and the ambiguity of form.

Since 1999, the kiss has been a recurring motif in Inez & Vinoodh’s work. More than a simple gesture, it represents for them a form of total union, the point at which two people nearly cease to be distinct from one another. The exhibition brings together several works from the “Me Kissing…” series, self-portraits of the couple kissing, alongside the brand-new “Think Love” (2025) series, which shows their son Charles kissing his partner Natalie under a red veil, photographed in the Texas desert, as if wrapped in a protective cocoon.

The exhibition “Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh” is on view at Kunstmuseum Den Haag, in The Hague (Netherlands), until September 6, 2026.

The book Can Love Be a Photograph — 40 Years of Inez & Vinoodh, published by Hannibal Books, is available for €69.95.

items.title: Jérémy Lempin: No One Is Supposed to Ignore Them
items.content:
In the aisle of a supermarket in northern France, a 74-year-old man holds a package at arm’s length, turns it over to check the date, then puts it back. Léon led a team for more than 30 years without ever learning to read. It is with this scene, as ordinary as it is disquieting, that Jérémy Lempin’s project opens.

There is something of the hush of a locker room in his images. One senses restrained gestures, faces composing themselves, hands hesitating over a notice or a form. Nothing spectacular, and the photographer is the first to say so, he who once led an entirely different life: he served aboard the aircraft carrier Charles-de-Gaulle, covered Operation Serval in Mali and Operation Sangaris in the Central African Republic, and received the Médaille Militaire from the hands of French President François Hollande before trading, in 2016, his non-commissioned officer’s cap for a photojournalist’s vest. One might expect such a background to lead toward the sensational. It does not. After the horse Peyo (World Press Photo, Visa d’or 2021) and the traumatized soldiers of Aux Armes et caetera, Jérémy Lempin chose this time to photograph what cannot be seen. The photographer says as much himself, plainly: he “does not photograph the spectacular but the ordinary,” and his images “force us to look at the daily lives of these anonymous people.”

Republic

In France, illiteracy was designated a national cause in 2013, and the label has lost none of its relevance: the French Senate raised concerns again this past April, and the National Agency for the Fight Against Illiteracy (ANLCI), whose presidency passes to Yves Rousset today, September 1, has just adopted five strategic priorities for 2025-2030. Founded in 2000, the agency remains the sole body tasked with coordinating efforts across the field, associations, the ministry of education, businesses. But the battleground is shifting: the near-total move to digital administrative procedures has turned a silent handicap into a permanent obstacle. Forms are no longer filled out at a counter; they are downloaded, signed online, verified through a digital portal. Every new online procedure closes the door a little further on those who have never been able to read it.

The choice of venue for the exhibition is no accident. The Cité internationale de la langue française, a museum dedicated to the French language, occupies the château of Villers-Cotterêts, the very place where, in 1539, King Francis I signed the ordinance making French the sole language of French administration and justice, sidelining the regional languages that had coexisted until then. Nearly five centuries later, exhibiting in its courtyard the faces of those who never gained full access to that language closes a bitter loop: the founding decree of French national unity also, unintentionally, drew the outline of those it would one day leave behind.

The figures, for their part, are unambiguous: 3.7 million adults educated in France struggle with basic skills, reading, writing, arithmetic, or 10.5% of the population aged 18 to 64. One in two is employed. One in two is over 45. And 71% of them spoke only French at home at age 5, which should put to rest, once and for all, the lazy equation between illiteracy and immigration.

Since 2023, Jérémy Lempin has followed these lives in the Nord region, in Marseille, in Paris, in Bordeaux and the Charente region, and in French Guiana, an overseas territory of France in South America, six regions where, he says, the divide is “most pronounced.” What links them has less to do with statistics than with a shared reticence turned into confession: Audrey, 40, a mother of three, goes back to school so as to no longer feel helpless in the face of her sons’ homework, and says she now feels “less of that sense of embarrassment, and that’s wonderful”; Angélique, 38, half-regrets not having “worked harder at school” while there was still time. This thwarted transmission plays out again, in reverse, with Élia, 50, in Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, French Guiana: she left school at 7, and it is her daughter Éliane, top of her class with a 17-out-of-20 average in a school where 9 out of 10 students struggle badly, who teaches her French every evening. “My nine children lack for nothing,” Élia says, “but I can’t help them with their homework.” Shakel, 27, embodies the other side of the same divide: with no other way out, he once swallowed 140 cocaine pellets; a digital outreach worker today, he speaks of his time in prison with a clarity that seeks neither excuse nor effect.

Others, across mainland France, have devised their own workarounds. Alain, 47, built himself a color-coded system to navigate daily life, down to an orange cross on his wall marking the family doctor’s number; to follow a recipe, he relies on video rather than text. Joëlle, a former school cook, is relearning arithmetic as an adult: after an hour spent applying a calculation to her grocery shopping, fatigue sets in, a sign of concentration her teacher says she rarely sees elsewhere, but she comes away with unmistakable pride, that of being able to shop on her own because she can now count. Later in the book, a postcard scrawled by 12-year-old Manfred during a summer learning camp closes the loop on childhood: a few clumsy words to his mother, whose very existence measures the distance he has traveled.

French Guiana, an overseas territory of France in South America, concentrates what the rest of the country would rather ignore: nearly 40% of adults there are illiterate, 39% of men and 43% of women, and three-quarters of them are unemployed. Residents of priority urban districts and of France’s overseas territories are 2.5 times more exposed than elsewhere; in the French Antilles and on Réunion Island, the phenomenon is three times more common than in mainland France. Twenty languages are spoken there, and written French competes directly with languages commonly spoken at home. Mariam Koita, an academic officer for illiteracy prevention at the Guiana education authority, notes that for many, “even though they were born in Guiana, French is not their native language.”

The principal of Paul Jean-Louis middle school, in Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, sums up in his own way the situation at a school built for 900 students that now enrolls 1,160: “Here, if you can’t read by first grade, you’re finished.” Three knife or gun attacks took place outside the school in 2023, one of them fatal. Reading a line like that, one grasps that illiteracy is never an isolated cause: it settles into the wreckage of something else, poverty, broken families, overcrowded schools, and lodges there for good.

Reticence

This concealment is one that everyone who works with adult learners knows by heart. In the book, Cécile Montastier, a program coordinator at the Greta-CFA Aquitaine training network in France, describes the first sentences she typically hears: “I’m not capable,” “I never understood, at school,” “I’m useless.” Many, she writes, learned very early to make themselves “as small as possible,” to go unnoticed in order to avoid judgment, until that discretion became an adult reflex. Shame, more than ignorance itself, is the real obstacle: it drives people to refuse help rather than be found out, turning a temporary gap into a lasting identity.

To tell the story of this ongoing concealment, Jérémy Lempin had the almost playful idea of using a Sprocket Rocket, an analog camera sold in supermarkets, which he bought for “barely 30 euros.” “I wanted to use something familiar,” he explains, drawn to a camera whose film exposes even its own sprocket holes: “It really shows the lack of resources and awareness in these regions and among the people concerned.” Looking at a portrait taken in French Guiana in which the subject’s face disappears behind one of those holes, he adds: “I see it a bit like a ‘no entry’ sign, because they were forbidden to speak their local language when French Guiana became a French overseas department.”

The book, prefaced by French novelist Marie-Hélène Lafon, brings together 150 photographs, handwritten letters written by the people Lempin met, who thus become co-authors, and texts signed by those working on the ground: the ANLCI, the association Mots & Merveilles, and Savoirs pour Réussir. Cécile Jaffré, director of the ANLCI, writes a line in the book that could sum up the whole project: “The image reveals what is invisible.” She also points out that, unlike other obstacles, this one is reversible: “You can learn, and relearn, at any age, provided you are given the means to do so.”

The object itself makes an argument of its own. Hardcover, 264 pages, FSC- and PEFC-certified paper, the title debossed on the cover: Hemeria, a French publishing house founded in 2018, describes the book as “a timeless, universal space of expression,” an object that “can be touched, kept, shared,” in contrast to the screen. The choice is not incidental for a subject that questions our very relationship to the written word: devoting such a carefully crafted volume to illiteracy is also a way of doing justice, through form, to those long kept at a distance from books.

Ignorance of the law is no excuse, the saying goes. In every image, Jérémy Lempin reminds us that 3.7 million people are, above all, unaware that they could, at last, stop being made invisible.

L’École de la vie. Liberté. Égalité. Invisibilité. (The School of Life. Liberty. Equality. Invisibility.) is published by Hemeria on September 4, opening the French National Days of Action Against Illiteracy. The accompanying exhibition is on view at the Cité internationale de la langue française in Villers-Cotterêts until September 20. The project is screened this Wednesday evening at Visa pour l’image, in Perpignan, and exhibited during the festival.

items.title: Taylor Galloway, Home Sweet Farm
items.content:
IN IMAGES

Taylor Galloway, Home Sweet Farm

For more than a decade, Los Angeles-based photographer Taylor Galloway returned to the family farm in Hartwood, Virginia, at a time when industrial agriculture is swallowing up small farms across the United States. From that unexpected welcome came across the street from Heaven, published by Deadbeat Club.

 

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Taylor Galloway.

An independent photographer, Taylor Galloway didn’t grow up in Virginia. Ten years ago, when he began this project, he met much of his grandmother’s family for the first time, she herself having grown up on the farm before moving away. Welcomed like one of their own, Galloway discovered there a sense of belonging he hadn’t expected. “The land has taught me everything,” he told the New York Times. “These are my people. This is where I come from.”

The images cultivate a vintage aesthetic without heavy-handed nostalgia: brown wood paneling, rotary phones, lace doilies and decorative plates, hymnals lined up side by side on a piano. Nothing here is staged for effect; everything simply seems to have stayed put, year after year, in this domestic cocoon where the beautiful and the trivial simply coexist. Most surprising of all, that reassuring familiarity doubles as a reassuring strangeness, embodied in a giant jigsaw puzzle of Bigfoot, an emblematic figure of American rural folklore, assembled with the gravity of a relic.

Among the many faces here: his grandmother, known as Gram; his great-aunt Bernice; his great-uncle Gene, who died six years before the book’s release, photographed in his kitchen alongside his dog Lulu after Sunday service; and Benjamin Dye, a fixture of the community and former starting right fielder for the 1958 Wichita Braves, photographed holding his old baseball glove. Simple, beautiful faces, strangely familiar, radiating a tenderness just beneath the skin.

The cover image, a night sky where the full moon hangs above silhouetted wildflowers, and the book’s poetic, promise-shaped title distill the project’s final intention, that of a native son come home, as in a fairy tale. According to the publisher, the book is not about “preserving the past, but about that which anchors the promise of a future, and the certainty of having found one’s way home.”

You close the book with the sense of having been given a seat at that table. And wondering whether, somewhere, you don’t have a farm of your own worth photographing.

across the street from Heaven, by Taylor Galloway, comes out in October from Deadbeat Club, with a special edition limited to 20 signed and numbered copies, including a chromogenic print and the 7″ vinyl The Hound Dog’s Hymn, a soundscape built from songs heard while working the farm.

items.title: Jean-François Leroy, Captain of Photojournalism, Dies at 69
items.content:
A former Sipa Press photographer, Jean-François Leroy served as editor-in-chief of Photo Magazine. Renowned for his editorial rigor and unwavering commitment to journalistic integrity, he was a Chevalier des Arts et Lettres and a Chevalier de l’Ordre du Mérite. Over nearly forty years, he turned Visa pour l’image into the world’s foremost gathering for photojournalism, free and open to the public, drawing more than 220,000 visitors to Perpignan every year: a platform for photographers working in the field, at odds with a news landscape he saw as increasingly driven by social media.

Just last year, for the festival’s 37th edition, he told Blind exactly why his fight still mattered: “Because the world is even more out of joint than usual, it has never needed Visa pour l’image more.” He summed up his conviction in a few simple words: “the world is in a bad way,” and the role he assigned to his profession: “journalism is a job on the front line of every piece of bad news on the planet.” He also denounced the overused word “objectivity” — “the first word we should banish from our journalistic folklore” — favoring instead a demand for honesty, and championed images “coming from the field, not from social media; images made by humans, not by [AI].”

A fellowship with photographers

That loyalty to the field also showed in the bonds Jean-François Leroy built with entire generations of photojournalists, many of whom, year after year, found their work exhibited or awarded in Perpignan.

Among them, Jean-Pierre Laffont, a longtime friend, whose decades covering the United States — where he first set foot in 1965 — were the subject of a retrospective at Visa last year. His wife Éliane and Jean-Pierre Laffont chose to share their grief upon hearing of his death, in a piece titled “Oh Captain! Our Captain!”:

“Dear Jean François, Jean Pierre and I have been your friends for 40 years, we were so young then, full of ideas, hope and ambition and with health that could withstand anything…. We could discuss photography all night and go to work in the morning without having had an hour of sleep… We did so many things together, photography festivals, books, shows… And in every corner of the planet… We also had some great laughs because you are the funniest friend I know, the most flamboyant too and the one with the biggest mouth!

You are the friend everyone should have, phenomenal, charismatic, spiritual, profound, curious, loyal, passionate and fascinating, you also have a great moral ethic and an immense sense of justice…You are the best, the greatest!

Jean François, you have changed the lives of thousands of photographers, including Jean Pierre. You are the first to have taken photojournalism out of the pages of newspapers and magazines and put it on walls, in churches, in convents, in the prisons of the city of Perpignan and I will always remember Jean-Pierre’s wonder and emotion when he saw his photos on those giant screens… Jean François, you changed the way people see the world and the way photographers see their work.

The world of photography without you is simply unimaginable. You are the captain, the lighthouse in the storm. I wish I could light up the Eiffel Tower and tell you what a beautiful light you are and that will remain in our lives.

Éliane and Jean-Pierre”

Sick, but at his post to the very end

Jean-François Leroy died Monday morning of cancer, surrounded by loved ones at his home in Paris. Despite his illness, he had taken part “from A to Z in preparing” this 38th edition, Delphine Lelu, managing director of Visa pour l’image, told the AFP news agency. “He is the soul of this festival, he carried it on his shoulders from the very first edition, in 1989. He leaves us a great legacy. He always wanted Perpignan to be a beacon for photojournalists, and we will make sure the festival keeps shining,” she added.

“The entire team of Visa pour l’image – Perpignan, and Jean-François Leroy’s whole family, are saddened to announce the death, this Monday, August 31, in the morning, of the founder and longtime director of the international photojournalism festival,” the festival announced on its Instagram account, honoring a man who “supported and showcased photojournalists from around the world.”

Axelle de Russé, a photojournalist honored several times at Visa pour l’Image for her reporting, and close to the man, also pays tribute to him, in these words: “Jean François Leroy. He wore that name so well. I think I can say that every one of us photojournalists grew up, matured, and dared, thanks to him, and to Visa pour l’Image. You come to Visa for the first time, intimidated, watching these big names from afar with admiration. Never daring to imagine that one day you might become part of that world. And then one day I got a phone call: “Axelle, it’s Jean François Leroy. You’ve won the Canon Female Photojournalist Award.” I thought it was a joke and hung up on him. We laughed about it for almost 20 years. Because we laughed with Jean François. He could be very tough, very critical of work you brought to show him. He impressed me. He had a sharp eye, an incredible talent for building a narrative. He knew how to tell stories, even the hardest ones. In 2020, I took part in what’s known as the schools’ week in Perpignan. There were 5 of us women photographers, and every day we gave middle-school classes tours of our exhibitions. I discovered a different man — funny, and generous. I don’t think I’ve ever laughed as much as I did that week. I can say it without hesitation: I am a photographer today because of him. Him, the irreverent one. He leaves us two days after the opening of the 38th edition. His tall silhouette, his slow gait, his glasses, his hat, his outbursts, his voice on the microphone, his unwavering commitment; the man embodied our profession, he was a symbol of photojournalism. We already miss him.”

The 38th edition of Visa pour l’image continues in Perpignan through September 13, 2026.

Cover image by Claude Truong-Ngoc.

items.title: Flowers of Speech
items.content:
In 1965, the poet Allen Ginsberg coined the phrase flower power to turn protest into peaceful spectacle. Two years later, photographer Bernie Boston made it an icon: a young man slipping a carnation into the barrel of a rifle at the foot of the Pentagon. Fifty-nine years have passed. The flower has not changed its name, but it has changed sides: it no longer disarms violence, it is now the object of an almost clinical suspicion. At the Jardin d’été in Arles, five artists brought together by Beata Nowak and Michel Poivert, curators of the project and authors of the book published by Textuel, no longer look to the flower for a symbol of peace. They look to it for clues.

Alice Pallot, a member of the Tendance Floue collective, followed architects Elena Seegers and Simon de Dreuille, founders of Botanical Agency, into the heart of a contradiction: floral foam, the material found in nearly every florist’s bouquet, becomes underwater “a persistent and pervasive source of pollution.” Pallot photographs the particles that break off it under horticultural LED light, invisible to the naked eye, revealed at last under a light designed to make things grow. The gesture is no laboratory accident, as the artist explains: “Bringing together scientists and artists is, for me, a way of making visible and understandable studies and articles that are sometimes impenetrable because of their inaccessible language.” After that, it is hard to look at a flower without looking at what makes it.

This same distrust of appearance drives Matei Bejenaru, who reaches back to the Brendel models, three-dimensional teaching aids made of papier-mâché, plaster, or wood, produced in Germany for the study of botany. He photographs them in color, almost like watercolors, where Karl Blossfeldt would have captured them in clinical black and white a century earlier. From a distance, the image reads as a plant. Up close, it reveals the artificiality of the replica. The doubt, for Bejenaru, is the point: it echoes a very real urgency, that of species now facing extinction.

Where Bejenaru plays on the confusion between plant and replica, Suzanne Lafont takes on a more ordinary form of blindness: the one we direct at the weeds of sidewalks, tree grates, and vacant lots. Twelve municipalities of Bordeaux Métropole on foot, plants placed on a light table to intensify their colors, then digitally inverted in reference to Goethe’s Theory of Colors. “Wild nature no longer exists,” the artist told the director of the Musée des Beaux-Arts in Bordeaux, where the work was first shown. What Lafont is fighting has a name: “plant blindness,” the cultural indifference to the vegetal world that lets us step over dozens of quiet lives every day.

The attention Lafont demands for urban weeds, Anaïs Tondeur carries even further, to the contaminated soils of the Land of Fires, near Naples, where toxic waste is buried. The plants that still grow there overproduce polyphenols, making it possible to create phytographs, chemical traces inscribed directly onto the emulsion. “Without extracting the plants from the soil, this photographic encounter takes place through nothing more than contact between the elements present,” the photographer explains. “It is one of the most environmentally respectful photographic protocols there is.” Philosopher Michael Marder then writes a letter to each plant; Tondeur reads it back to them; a second phytograph is born from that reading.

This correspondence between the human and the vegetal finds an even more intimate echo in the work of Jiang Zhi, who sets flowers alight in full bloom for his series 情书 (Love Letters), dedicated to the memory of his wife Ren Lan, whose name means “orchid” in Chinese. Ikebana, the Japanese art of embracing the ephemeral, is here subverted: the burning flower no longer seeks eternity, it sets fire to it. “The fire is as beautiful as the flower, and the flower too is entirely without flaw,” the artist says, “but of course, this is only a temporary beauty.” The flower burns. The love letter remains.

“Flower Power” runs through October 4, 2026, in the Jardin d’été, as part of the Rencontres d’Arles. Catalogue published by Textuel and available for €59.
items.excerpt: Five artists and one motif: the flower, long confined to ornament, becomes the ground for an inquiry into the living world in Arles. “Flower Power” unfolds its paper petals through October 4.

items.title: Dust and Decibels: Rave on Film
items.content:
You can feel it: these two women lived the rave from within. It was woven into their daily lives, anchored by ritual, carried by tribe. A mosaic of faces and figures caught in the grain of the film: closed eyes, a bride in a tulle veil toasting amid a circle of laughing friends, half-smiles of ecstasy wrung out at dawn while the bassline pounds on. The book stands as an ode to the great family of the free party, in all its European guises: from Italy to the Czech Republic, where CzechTek drew crowds in the thousands, by way of the Basque Country and the Provençal countryside around Aix-en-Provence.

That family, Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi first came to know separately. They crossed paths on the benches of the same art school in Milan, long before truly meeting in the mud and feedback of a wall of speakers. Both were already taking photographs, each in her own way, before finding common ground. “We had two different ways of looking at things, even though we were experiencing the same parties and were often together,” Cheyenne recalls. “One of us might be drawn to a face or a particular situation, while the other would be attracted to something completely different. And yet today, our photographs blend together perfectly.”

From this alchemy between two eyes, no individual signature remains: throughout the book, the photographers chose never to specify who took which picture. “Maybe that’s exactly the point,” Valentina suggests: “two different perspectives that, over time, became a shared memory.” A deliberate anonymity, true to the spirit of the movement it immortalises. The book is equally striking for its total absence of visual hierarchy. A wall of speakers is photographed with the same gravity as a child playing with a dog in the dust of an encampment. “It tells exactly what we experienced: situations, speakers, trucks, children, dogs and people.”

That levelling of gaze builds, page after page, into the portrait of an entire life rather than a mere nocturnal pastime. Bodies stretched out by the water, a black dog standing sentinel before a tower of speakers, whole convoys of camper vans lined up on some improvised lot. “For more than seven years, we lived on four wheels, in trucks, moving between the road and squatted social centres. Never Alone is infused with that sense of freedom and community that defined our lives,” Cheyenne and Valentina explain. The sound system here is no mere party backdrop, but an itinerant domestic architecture in which the speaker stack stands in for the hearth, the truck for the sitting room, and the road for a permanent address.

That happy nomadism, though, sits at odds with another constant running through the book, one that reads as stranger still today: the almost benevolent presence of the police. It is hard, from where we stand now, to picture a uniform ever blending into the scenery of a free party. And yet even in the rare frames where law enforcement meets the lens, no tension shows on any face. “What we experienced at the end of the 1990s can never be repeated,” they observe. “The police didn’t really know how to deal with us yet, and we were living in a time that was far less controlled than today. Now algorithms, cameras and surveillance permeate every aspect of our lives.”

Children of the Bassline

That sense of a lost innocence finds a pointed echo in the book’s foreword, written by Tobia D’Onofrio, who suggests that the children pictured here may be the very same young people now protesting against the authorities. In France, several bills aimed at further criminalising free parties are currently under consideration, following in the wake of the anti-rave decree passed by the Meloni government in late 2022. It is a lineage the photographers acknowledge without grandstanding. “Free-party culture hasn’t disappeared, and fortunately the new generations haven’t allowed themselves to be intimidated. Illegal rave parties are still being organised, less frequently and a little more under the radar, and we can only be happy about that.”

And yet this continuity, however reassuring, raises an almost vertiginous question about the photographic act itself. The American writer Hakim Bey once theorised the rave as a “temporary autonomous zone,” a gesture designed by its very nature to vanish. Photography does precisely the opposite: it arrests time, fixes it onto a light-sensitive surface. Isn’t there something paradoxical in that? The two women wave the objection away with disarming simplicity. “When we took those photographs, our intention wasn’t to ‘document’ anything. We both had a passion for photography, and for us these were simply images of our everyday lives.”

That same absence of calculation runs through their choice of medium: there is no retro affectation behind the exclusive use of black and white. “It was an editorial choice, since most of the photographs were originally shot in black and white. We have always loved black-and-white film. We also used to print the photographs ourselves in the darkroom, using an enlarger.”

Out of that artisanal darkroom labour, certain images resurface with particular force. “Every photograph brings something back and stirs something in me,” Cheyenne confides. Valentina, for her part, remembers with precision Tequinox, a party held in Bologna in 1999: “We found the location for the party only a few days before it began, thinking it was abandoned. Several sound systems arrived, along with people from all over Europe.” One senses that night in one of the book’s photographs: a square overrun with vans and huddled figures beneath a low sky, where you can almost feel the bass still trembling underfoot.

In the end, the party itself was only ever the backdrop to something larger: the wanderings of a generation in perpetual motion, for whom the collective was the answer. Few places remain today where such lives would still be possible. The free party endures as one of the last spaces of self-organised, collective and free celebration, and it is precisely for that reason that it finds itself, across Europe, in the crosshairs of politics.

All images: © Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, Courtesy of and published by DRAGO

Never Alone: 1997-2004 Raving in Europe, by Cheyenne Clementi and Valentina Morandi, is published by Drago Propaganda, 196 pages, €60. Available at www.neveralonebook.it
